title: History of AI
description: The story of AI is not a smooth line of progress. It is a story of breakthrough, overpromise, and recovery. Understanding this history helps you recognize what AI can and cannot do today.
learningObjectives: Explain why AI is older than most people think
Describe why AI experienced two 'winters' of reduced funding
Identify the key breakthrough that started modern AI
Recognize why history helps you evaluate current AI claims

opening.hook: You might think AI is a recent invention. The term was actually coined in 1956—before the internet, before personal computers, before most of us were born. So why did it take over 60 years for AI to become what it is today?
opening.relevance: Understanding this history helps you see why AI is both more impressive and more limited than headlines suggest.

content.content: In 1950, a British mathematician named Alan Turing asked a question that would shape the next 75 years of computing: 'Can machines think?'

Turing did not try to answer this directly. Instead, he proposed a test. If you talked to a machine through text and could not tell whether you were talking to a human or a machine, then for practical purposes, the machine was intelligent.

content.definition: A test of whether a machine's responses can be indistinguishable from a human's.
content.example: If you exchange messages with a system for 5 minutes and cannot tell whether it is human or AI, it has passed the test.

content.content: Six years later, in 1956, a group of researchers met at Dartmouth College. They believed they could make significant progress on AI in a single summer. One of them, John McCarthy, coined the term 'Artificial Intelligence' for the conference.

content.reality: AI as a field is almost 70 years old. The term was coined in 1956.

content.content: The 1960s were full of optimism. Researchers promised machine translation, general problem solvers, and human-level AI within a generation. None of these arrived on time.
When results failed to materialize, funding dried up. This happened twice—periods now called 'AI Winters.'

content.definition: A period of reduced funding and interest in AI research after expectations were not met.
content.example: The first AI Winter (1974-1980) followed the failure of machine translation programs to deliver practical results.

content.before: 1960s promise: 'We will have human-level AI in 20 years.'
content.after: 1970s reality: 'Our systems can solve toy problems but fail on real ones.'

content.content: The second AI Winter (1987-1993) followed the collapse of the 'expert systems' market. Expert systems encoded human rules into software—useful, but expensive to maintain and brittle when situations changed.

content.myth: AI just keeps getting better every year.
content.reality: AI has experienced multiple periods of stagnation. Progress is not guaranteed—it depends on funding, breakthroughs, and realistic expectations.

content.content: For decades, AI systems relied on hand-coded rules. Researchers had to specify every detail. This approach worked for narrow problems but could not scale to messy, real-world data.

Then, in 2012, a system called AlexNet entered the ImageNet competition—a challenge to classify millions of images into 1000 categories. AlexNet did not use hand-coded rules. It used a deep neural network that learned patterns directly from the data.

content.title: AlexNet wins ImageNet 2012
content.significance: AlexNet outperformed the second-best system by over 10 percentage points. This was not incremental improvement—it was a fundamental shift.
content.impact: Within 3 years, nearly all competitive systems used deep learning.

content.content: The reason was not new ideas. Neural networks had existed since the 1950s. What changed was data (the internet) and compute (GPUs). Deep learning finally had enough of both.

The transformer architecture (2017) was a particularly important milestone. It allowed models to process language much more effectively than earlier approaches. Every major AI model today—GPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek—is built on transformers.

content.myth: ChatGPT is the beginning of AI.
content.reality: ChatGPT is the result of 60+ years of research, with a key breakthrough (transformers) in 2017 and a landmark product launch in 2022.

keyTakeaways: AI as a field is nearly 70 years old — the term was coined in 1956.
Progress has not been linear — AI experienced two 'winters' of reduced funding.
Deep learning succeeded because data and compute finally became available.
The transformer architecture (2017) enabled the modern AI boom.
Understanding AI history helps you evaluate current AI claims critically.

reflection.prompt: Given this history, why do you think people often overestimate what AI can do today?
reflection.hint: Consider the pattern of overpromise followed by disappointment.
reflection.expectedInsight: Because AI progress is not steady — it comes in bursts, and enthusiasm often outpaces realistic capability.

items.question: Which of these is the most accurate description of AI's history?
options: Periods of progress interrupted by AI Winters
items.explanation: AI has not progressed in a straight line. It experienced two 'winters' when funding and interest dropped, followed by renewed progress driven by new breakthroughs.
items.whyItMatters: Understanding this pattern helps you evaluate current AI claims — enthusiasm often outpaces capability.

items.question: Why did deep learning suddenly start working in 2012?
options: A new algorithm was invented in 2012
Neural networks were finally proven mathematically
Data and compute became available at scale
items.explanation: Neural networks existed since the 1950s. What changed in 2012 was access to massive data (the internet) and powerful compute (GPUs).
items.whyItMatters: Many AI breakthroughs are enabled by resources, not just ideas. This helps you understand why AI is booming now rather than 30 years ago.

items.question: In your own words, why is AI history relevant to understanding AI today?
items.answer: Because AI's pattern of overpromise followed by disappointment repeats. Understanding history helps you distinguish between real breakthroughs and hype.
items.explanation: History provides context for evaluating current AI claims. If a new AI product sounds too good to be true, the history of AI suggests caution.
items.whyItMatters: This is the core skill for responsible AI use — thinking critically about what AI claims actually mean.

items.question: A headline says: 'New AI model achieves human-level reasoning.' Based on AI history, what questions should you ask?
items.answer: 1. What does 'human-level reasoning' actually mean? 2. On which benchmark? 3. Who is evaluating? 4. What are the limitations? 5. Is this overpromise similar to past AI promises?
items.explanation: History shows that 'human-level' claims have appeared before and often turn out to be benchmark-specific rather than general.
items.whyItMatters: This is the transfer of historical knowledge to real-world evaluation.

notes.summary: AI is almost 70 years old. It has experienced breakthroughs and winters. Deep learning succeeded because data and compute finally became available. Transformers (2017) enabled the modern boom.

importantTerms.definition: A test of machine intelligence based on indistinguishable responses.
A period of reduced AI funding after failed promises.
The neural network architecture behind modern AI models.

notes.reflection: AI's history shows that enthusiasm and hype are not the same as capability.
